hook: Two bars on a graph: 0.46 and 0.62. The second is taller, but is it really different, or would another eight beet cubes flip the order? Error bars answer that at a glance, and on the exam you will be asked both to draw them and to say what they show.

prereq.q: What is the standard error of a mean with s = 0.30 and n = 9?
What does a selectively permeable membrane do?
options: Lets some substances cross easily while blocking or slowing others
Lets every dissolved substance cross at the same speed
Blocks water while letting large charged molecules through
prereq.why: The hydrophobic core and specific proteins let small nonpolar molecules (and water through aquaporins) cross, while large or charged molecules are held back.

prereq.q: An experiment shows a difference far larger than chance variation. What do you do with the null hypothesis?
prereq.why: A difference too large to blame on chance leads you to reject the null hypothesis.

figure.caption: With 95% confidence interval error bars: no overlap, the difference is likely real (reject the null); overlap, the data do not show a difference (fail to reject).

chain.cause: A sample mean is only an estimate of the true mean, and its uncertainty is measured by SE = s ÷ √n.
chain.effect: You can build a range around it that very probably contains the true mean.

chain.cause: About 95% of sample means fall within 2 standard errors of the true mean.
chain.effect: The interval x̄ ± 2SE is an approximate 95% confidence interval.

chain.cause: You draw that interval as an error bar on each plotted mean.
chain.effect: A reader can see how precisely each mean is known.

chain.cause: Two groups' 95% CI error bars do not overlap.
chain.effect: The difference is unlikely to be chance: it is statistically significant, and you reject the null hypothesis.
The data do not show a difference, so you fail to reject the null; more data could still reveal one.

ideas: Worked example. 15 °C: n = 9, x̄ = 1.8, s = 0.30, SE = 0.10, CI = 1.6-2.0. 25 °C: n = 9, x̄ = 2.5, s = 0.36, SE = 0.12, CI = 2.26-2.74. No overlap: likely a real difference.
Formula sheet: SE = s ÷ √n; 95% CI ≈ x̄ ± 2SE. A bigger sample gives a smaller SE and a narrower interval.
Overlap rule (95% CI bars only): no overlap, likely a real difference; overlap, the data do not show one. Overlap never proves the means are equal.
Always say what your error bars show (SD, SE or 95% CI). The same picture means different things for each.

misconception.wrong: If two 95% confidence interval error bars overlap, the two means are the same.
misconception.right: Overlap means only that the data do not show a difference at this level of confidence. A real difference can hide behind overlapping bars, especially with small samples.

summary: A 95% confidence interval, about x̄ ± 2SE, is a range that very probably contains the true mean; drawn on a graph it becomes an error bar. If two groups' 95% CI bars do not overlap, the difference is statistically significant and the null hypothesis is rejected. If they overlap, the data do not show a difference, which is not the same as showing there is none. Larger samples narrow the intervals. Always label what error bars represent.
